title: Blue Valley Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Blue Valley wells have a 300 ft median depth, with typical drilling costs of $65-$100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock.
intro_html:
Buying mountain property in Blue Valley means understanding the ground below the lot. Records within 5 miles show wells in fractured mountain bedrock, with a median completed depth of 300 feet and a median reported yield of 7.0 gallons per minute.

The records are useful for setting expectations, but they are not a guarantee for a particular parcel. Drilling results can change sharply across short distances in granite and gneiss. Nearby wells, access, septic design, water rights, and the intended household use all belong in the purchase and building review.

sections.heading: Blue Valley well depths reflect fractured mountain ground
sections.html:
Blue Valley wells have a median reported depth of 300 feet. The middle half runs from 180 to 460 feet, so a driller bidding a typical lot should not assume a shallow hole. Forty percent of wells fall between 300 and 600 feet, while 14% are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest recorded well is 3,523 feet.

That spread is consistent with mountain bedrock, where fractures control both drilling progress and water entry. The permit records identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 2,517 wells, with smaller groups listed as Fractured Crystalline and Fractured Granite. Wells in Floyd Hill, Idaho Springs, Pine Valley, Upper Witter Gulch, and Echo Hills can provide useful comparison points, but the closest neighboring wells are more important than a broad area average.

sections.heading: Most Blue Valley wells produce usable household flow
sections.html:
Among the wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 7.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces 4.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute, and 64% falls between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. Those results are generally workable for a home when the pressure system, storage, and plumbing are designed correctly.

Only 1% of reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, but a low-yield result can still be a serious constraint on a specific lot. A yield test is not the same as unlimited supply. Ask for the well completion report, pump test information, storage-tank size, and any records of recovery after pumping. An exempt household-use well is generally limited to 35 gallons per minute under Colorado rules, and water use must still match the permit.

sections.heading: Water levels are deeper now than older measurements
sections.html:
The median static water level is 95 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 49 to 150 feet. That measurement describes where water stood when the well was checked, not the depth of the well and not necessarily the level during extended pumping.

The decade figures show a change worth investigating. The median measured level was 45 feet below surface in the 1970s, compared with 110 feet in both the 2010s and 2020s. That pattern is consistent with deeper measured water levels in the later records, although only 92 wells report a static water level and the measurements may come from different locations and conditions. A buyer should compare the actual neighboring wells rather than treating the series as a parcel-specific forecast.

sections.heading: Permit history runs from Idaho Springs to the newer records
sections.html:
Colorado DWR permit records contain 2,588 wells in this five-mile area. Of those, 1,670 are recorded as constructed, 1,629 report a total depth, and 881 report a pump yield. The permit history is concentrated in several periods: 588 permits were issued in the 1970s and 615 in the 1990s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The most frequently listed drillers are James Drilling Company, associated with Keaton and Michael K., with 302 records; Walton with 163; and Living Water Systems Inc., associated with Goble and Robert, with 155. These names describe historical permit records, not a recommendation or proof that a contractor is available for a new project. Confirm current licensing, insurance, references, and scope before hiring.

sections.heading: A 300-foot Blue Valley well starts around $19,500 to drill
sections.html:
In Blue Valley's fractured granite and gneiss, the modeled drilling rate is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $19,500 to $30,000. A finished well, including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work, is modeled at about $25,500 to $42,000.

Those figures are planning ranges, not a guaranteed bid. Depth is the largest obvious variable, but access for the rig, casing and grout requirements, water testing, pump selection, trench length, and power work can change the total. Ask for a written allowance for additional footage and clarify what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than the target yield.

sections.heading: Mines, PFAS sites, and mountain construction need review
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information within about 10 miles includes 15 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2,838 historic mine features, and 15 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped features do not prove that a particular well is contaminated, but they are a reason to review the parcel's location, historic land use, drainage, and available water-quality tests.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured bedrock even where nearby wells perform well. Test for bacteria and other constituents appropriate to the site, and ask a qualified professional to interpret the results. Septic setbacks, replacement-area requirements, steep access, trenching, and foundation work should be checked before closing. A good well does not by itself make a lot buildable.

sections.heading: Check the well, water rights, and building plan before buying
sections.html:
Start with the DWR permit and completion report for the property, then locate the nearest comparable wells. Compare depths, yields, static levels, pump equipment, and construction dates. For a home purchase, have the well flow and pressure tested and obtain current water-quality testing rather than relying on a neighbor's result.

Confirm that the permit authorizes the intended use. Domestic and household wells make up 88% of the records, while monitoring wells account for 8%; a permit's location in the database does not automatically establish the water rights or uses you need. If the lot is in an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may be required. Before building, coordinate the well, septic system, driveway, electrical service, and emergency access as one site plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Blue Valley, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Blue Valley is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 180 to 460 feet, while 14% of wells are 600 feet or deeper. The deepest record is 3,523 feet. Fractured granite and gneiss make depth vary substantially between nearby lots, so neighboring completion reports are more useful than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Blue Valley?
faq.a: The modeled drilling rate in Blue Valley's fractured mountain bedrock is $65 to $100 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, drilling the hole is about $19,500 to $30,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is modeled at about $25,500 to $42,000. Access and final depth can move the bid outside that range.

faq.q: How much water do Blue Valley wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported pump yield is 7.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 4.0 to 10.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-four percent of reported wells produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute. One percent report less than 1 gallon per minute. A pump test and storage evaluation are still needed for the specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Blue Valley, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that water is safe for drinking. Within about 10 miles, mapped information includes 15 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 2,838 historic mine features, and 15 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property's water for bacteria and site-appropriate contaminants, then have qualified professionals interpret the results before relying on it.

faq.q: Are Blue Valley well water levels getting lower?
faq.a: Reported median static water levels were 45 feet below surface in the 1970s and 110 feet below surface in both the 2010s and 2020s. That suggests deeper measured water levels in later records, but only 92 wells report static levels and conditions vary by location. Review the property's own measurements and nearby wells before drawing a firm conclusion.
